concerns: Web check NOT done (web search limit used up).
'Weather' will make people expect a weather, climate or ambient/ASMR channel, and it may be filed with weather content.
The weakest link to borders and empires. The proposer agrees the tagline would have to carry it.

round1.name: Chamberstick
round1.why: A chamberstick is the short candle holder with a ring handle that people carried up the stairs to bed for centuries. It matches the single-candle logo exactly, means 'the light you take to bed in the old days', is one easy word, and leaves room for any era.
concerns: The web check was not run because the shared web search budget for this turn ran out (200 searches). Books, podcasts, companies, apps and trademarks using this name are unknown. By the rules, an unverified name does not survive.

It is a common antiques word, so a web search for it will show antique candle holders for sale before the channel. That is mostly a discoverability problem, not a legal one, but the channel will have to earn the top result.
Many people do not know the word. Heard once, it may be typed as 'Chamber Stick' or 'Chamberstik'. Getting the spaced handle as well would help.
Small businesses such as antique, candle and gift shops may well use it. A web search should look for these before the name is used.

round1.name: Banked Embers
round1.why: Banking the fire, covering the coals with ash so they last till morning, was the last job of the night in old homes. It feels warm and hushed and suggests something that glows slowly for hours, like the videos.
concerns: The web check was not run because the web search budget ran out. This is a natural phrase that is likely already used as a novel or story title, a candle scent, a band or album name, or a bar or restaurant name. None of these could be ruled out.
'Banked' also brings banks and money to mind, which pulls slightly against the cosy meaning.
It works more as a mood than as a history channel name; on its own it says sleep or cosiness, not the past.

round1.name: Lantern Clock
round1.why: The lantern clock was the household clock of the 1600s, a brass clock with a slow single hand. It joins time and soft light, suits multi-hour videos, and fits a candle logo without using the word.
concerns: The web check was not run because the web search budget ran out.
It is a standard term for a type of antique clock, so web and YouTube searches will fill with clock dealers, auction listings and clock-repair videos. The channel would struggle to own the name.
A generic product term is weak to defend as a brand. Clock, watch and app makers could also use it.
'Clock' suggests alarms and waking up, which pulls against sleep.

round1.name: Thatch and Tallow
round1.why: Thatched roofs and tallow lights, the stuff of ordinary homes before electricity. It says 'everyday life in the past' without the worn words, sounds soft, is easy to remember, and stretches from a Roman bakery to a medieval cottage. A web search found no business or title with this name.
concerns: The web check was not run because the web search budget ran out. The proposer's claim that the name is unused could not be confirmed. 'X & Tallow' is a very common pattern for tallow skincare, soap and candle makers, so a small shop with this name is quite likely.
'Tallow' is rendered animal fat. Some listeners will find that unappealing, and it suggests skincare products more than bedtime stories.
The 'and' makes people unsure how to type it (&, 'n', and), and the handle runs together as ThatchandTallow.
It sounds like a pub, a craft shop or a homesteading channel more than a sleep channel.

round1.name: Ages Abed
round1.why: 'Ages' for history, 'abed' (old English for 'in bed') for sleep: the whole idea in two short words, said in one breath. Small risk: Abed is also a given name, so a few people may first read it as a name.
concerns: The web check was not run because the web search budget ran out.
Many people will read 'Abed' as a name, and in English-speaking media it is best known as the character Abed in the sitcom Community. 'Ages, Abed' can read like a line spoken to him.
Heard aloud it is easily misheard as 'Ages Ahead', which means the opposite (the future) and sends people to other searches.
'Abed' is an archaic word that many viewers will not know. Run together as 'agesabed', the handle is hard to read.

round1.name: Sandglass Hours
round1.why: Sandglass is the old word for an hourglass. With 'hours' it suggests time running slowly and long videos, and it is calm and easy to say. It points less clearly to history than the names above.
concerns: The web check was not run because the web search budget ran out. 'Sandglass' is used by several products and businesses, which a search would need to rule out.
It hardly suggests history and sounds more like a meditation, focus-timer or productivity app.
The image of sand running out suggests deadlines and time slipping away more than rest.
People may type 'Hourglass Hours' or 'Sand Glass Hours'.

round1.name: Wax and Wattle
round1.why: Wattle-and-daub walls and wax lights: humble materials of old homes, so it points to ordinary life in the past. It is a gentle sound pair and easy to type.
concerns: The web check was not run because the web search budget ran out. Wattle is Australia's national flower, and 'Wax & Wattle' sounds very much like an Australian candle or soap shop, so a clash with a small business is likely.
'Wattle' is also the loose skin under a turkey's (or a person's) neck, an unflattering image.
Few people know wattle-and-daub. As with Thatch and Tallow, the 'and' makes it unclear how to type it.
It reads as a craft or candle brand, not a sleep history channel.

round1.name: Curfew Embers
round1.why: 'Curfew' comes from the medieval couvre-feu, the evening bell that told every house to cover its fire for the night. That makes a lovely tagline story. Small drawback: 'curfew' also has a modern 'rules' feel.
concerns: The web check was not run because the web search budget ran out.
'Curfew' now means police curfews, lockdowns, unrest and teenagers grounded. Those are rules and punishment, the opposite of a soothing bedtime.
The couvre-feu story needs explaining before the name makes sense; without it the words just sit side by side.
It could be read as a game, a band or a dystopian novel title.

tagline: Real cases. Told from the record.

round1.name: Wax Impression
round1.why: It means the mark a seal leaves in wax, which is your red-seal logo. It is also the old thief's trick of pressing a key into wax to copy it, which is how the 1855 Great Gold Robbery was done. It sounds sober and archival, and it is quietly about heists.
concerns: Fails the 'unsure means out' rule only because the web check could not be done; this is the best name of the eight on merit
'Wax impression' is an everyday term in dentistry, locksmithing and jewellery casting, so web and Google results will be crowded with those and the phrase is hard to own as a trademark
From memory, not verified: wax-seal stamp shops and vinyl record sellers ('wax' is slang for records) plausibly trade as 'Wax Impression(s)'; this needs checking
'Impression' can also suggest comedy impressions or 'first impressions'

round1.name: Ink and Gall
round1.why: Iron gall ink is the ink most old court records were written in. Gall also means brazen nerve, the thing every swindler and hoaxer needs. Half the name is the record and half is the crook.
concerns: Not web-checked, so it is out under the 'unsure means out' rule
Weak radio test: heard once, it can come out as 'Ink and Gaul', 'Inc and Gal' or 'Ink and Gold', and people won't know whether to write 'and', '&' or 'n'
The iron-gall-ink meaning is obscure, so most viewers will only get the 'gall' (nerve) half
From memory, not verified: calligraphy-ink makers and tattoo studios often use 'ink' and 'gall' names, so a small business conflict is likely

round1.name: Wax and Warrant
round1.why: Sealing wax and the warrant stand for the document and the law catching up. It suits the logo, has a firm sound for a sober brand and leaves room for any era or crime type.
concerns: Not web-checked, so it is out under the 'unsure means out' rule
Echoes 'wax and wane', so listeners may hear or remember it as 'Wax and Wane'; 'Warrant' can be heard as 'Warren'
The 'X and Y' pattern sounds like a candle shop, barber or bar, so it is generic and easy to confuse with small businesses (likely ones exist; unverified)
'Warrant' is also the name of a well-known 1980s glam-metal band; a minor overlap

round1.name: Hand and Seal
round1.why: It comes from 'given under my hand and seal', the formula that made old deeds and depositions official. It describes the logo exactly, a signed document with a red seal. It is short and passes the radio test easily. A small risk is that it could be mistaken for a notary business.
concerns: Not web-checked, so it is out under the 'unsure means out' rule

It is a standard legal formula, so notary, apostille and document-signing businesses very plausibly use it (the proposer flagged this too); a legal-services brand under the same name would knock it out
'Hand seals' is a very well-known term in the anime Naruto (ninja hand signs), which will crowd search results; 'seal' also brings up the animal
Says nothing about crime, frauds or heists; a viewer would not guess the genre

round1.name: Court Hand
round1.why: Court hand was the handwriting used in English legal records for centuries. It is a deep-cut archival name with a second reading: the hand of the court. Its weakness is that some people may hear it as a sports or job term at first.
concerns: Not web-checked, so it is out under the 'unsure means out' rule
An obscure palaeography term: few viewers will know it, and many will hear a sports term (tennis or basketball court) or a job title (like 'farm hand'), as the proposer admits
As a historical script it is likely used for fonts and archive teaching material, so it is generic and hard to own (unverified)
The handle 'CourtHand' can be misread as 'Cour Thand'

round1.name: Sealed and Sworn
round1.why: Every source the channel uses was sealed or sworn. It is calm and trustworthy, it suits the red seal, and it signals that this is a record-based retelling rather than sensational.
concerns: Not web-checked, so it is out under the 'unsure means out' rule
Listeners will easily swap the order ('Sworn and Sealed') and look up the wrong handle
Echoes 'Signed, Sealed, Delivered' and sounds like a romance or fantasy novel title or a legal-services firm; such titles plausibly exist (unverified)
Generic and doesn't signal frauds, heists or hoaxes

round1.name: Witness Whereof
round1.why: It comes from 'In witness whereof', the line at the end of sworn and sealed documents, just before the signature and seal. It is exact and archival, it suits the wax-seal logo, and it promises testimony on the record rather than gore.
concerns: Not web-checked, so it is out under the 'unsure means out' rule; 'In Witness Whereof' is a stock legal phrase likely used for book titles and legal blogs (unverified)
Without 'In' the name reads like a cut-off phrase
'Whereof' is archaic and easily misspelled ('Wherof', 'Where of', 'Wearof')
'Witness' is heavily used in true-crime titles and suggests murder testimony rather than frauds and hoaxes

round1.name: Writ and Ruse
round1.why: A writ is the court's paper and a ruse is the con. Together they describe every episode: a fraud or hoax rebuilt from the documents. YouTube's channel search returned no channels at all for it.
concerns: Not web-checked, so it is out under the 'unsure means out' rule
Fails the radio test: the silent W and 'ruse' make it sound like 'Rit and Roos' or 'Rit and Rues', so someone who hears it once can't type it
Sounds like a weaker 'Rhyme and Reason'
The empty search result shows it is unused, not that it is good

tagline: Contracts, cover and closings, in plain English.

round1.name: Paperwork Atlas
round1.why: It presents the channel as a map of confusing paperwork, one term or document per page, which leaves plenty of room to grow into new document types. It's plain to type and reassuring in tone.
concerns: Web check (step 2) not done, so it can't be trusted completely yet and doesn't survive under the 'unsure means out' rule.
'Atlas' appears in a great many brand names (software, publishing, travel), so the name may be hard to own in search and trademark, and it may sound like a document-management app.
'Paperwork' suggests drudgery, though the channel exists to ease it.
Strengths: easy to type after hearing it once, no bad meaning in English or Spanish, covers legal, insurance and real-estate papers, and leaves room to grow.

round1.name: Deeds and Deductibles
round1.why: It names a real-estate document and an insurance term together, so viewers know the subject at once, and the alliteration makes it easy to remember and say. It's a bit more literal than the names above, and legal topics such as liens and leases sit under it comfortably.
concerns: Web check not done, so it doesn't survive.
Reads like the name of an insurance agency or title company, so a small local firm may already use it (unverified), and it could imply the channel sells a service.
'Deeds' also means good deeds, a small ambiguity.
19-character handle; viewers may type an '&' or 'Deductables'.

round1.name: Whereas and Wherefore
round1.why: 'Whereas' opens the background section of contracts and 'wherefore' means 'why', so the name promises the background and the reason behind every term. It sounds tidy and well-read, it's easy to spell after hearing it once, and it covers legal, insurance and real-estate papers alike.
concerns: Web check not done, so it doesn't survive.
Easily misheard as the common idiom 'the whys and wherefores', which other blogs, podcasts or businesses probably use (unverified), so viewers may type the wrong name.
Many people think 'wherefore' means 'where' (from Romeo and Juliet), so the meaning behind the name is lost on most of them.
Archaic legalese is at odds with a plain-English promise.

round1.name: The Signing Table
round1.why: It's the table where people sign a lease, a closing packet or an insurance policy, and that's the moment they most need the terms made clear. It reassures without giving advice ('pull up a chair before you sign'), fits all three subjects, and suits a magnifying glass over a page.
concerns: Web check not done, so it doesn't survive.

Generic phrase also used for wedding guest-book tables and book signings, and a likely name for notary or loan-signing-agent businesses (unverified). It's descriptive, so it's hard to own in search or trademark.
Could suggest the channel attends closings or acts as a notary, which blurs the 'education only, never advice' line.
35 channels in search shows a crowded result space.

round1.name: Termwright
round1.why: A wright is a skilled maker, so a termwright is someone who crafts terms into something readable. It's distinctive and fully ownable (YouTube search returned no channels). Radio risk: a listener may type 'Termright', so the second-choice handle should be claimed as well.
concerns: Web check not done, so it doesn't survive.
Fails the 'hear it once, type it' test: 'Termright', 'Termwrite' and 'Term Rite' are all likely spellings, so you'd need to defend several handles.
Sounds like a surname-based law firm ('Wright'), which may suggest legal services.
'Term' also suggests term life insurance or school terms.

round1.name: Now Therefore
round1.why: 'NOW, THEREFORE' is the turn in a contract where the background ends and the actual terms begin. As a name it says 'now you understand it, so you can read on with confidence'. It sounds calm and orderly, and it isn't tied to any one subject.
concerns: Web check not done, so it doesn't survive.
'Now therefore' is a frequent Bible and sermon phrase, so search results will likely be crowded with religious content and ministries may use it (unverified).
Sounds like a sentence fragment, and newcomers can't tell the subject from it.
Viewers may type 'Now Therefor'.

round1.name: Glossworthy
round1.why: A gloss is an explanatory note written between the lines of a text, which is exactly what the logo shows, and the '-worthy' ending echoes 'trustworthy'. It's short, easy to say and spell, ownable (YouTube search returned no channels at all), and it doesn't tie the channel to one kind of document. One risk: some people may think of lip gloss at first.
concerns: Web check not done, so it doesn't survive.
Bad meaning for this channel: to 'gloss over' means to skim past or hide something, the opposite of a channel built on clarity and trust.
The lip gloss and 'glossy' (superficial) associations are strong, and it sounds like a cosmetics, nail or detailing brand, so beauty businesses may well use it (unverified).
The scholarly meaning of 'gloss' is unknown to most viewers.

round1.name: Terms and Teacups
round1.why: It sets dry terms beside a calming cup of tea, which signals that the explanations are unhurried and friendly. 'Terms' covers legal, insurance and real-estate vocabulary alike. It's warmer and more playful than the others, which some owners will prefer and some won't.
concerns: Web check not done, so it doesn't survive.
Sounds like a cozy lifestyle or tea channel; the requested tone is 'tidy, trustworthy', not whimsical.
Could be typed as 'Terms and Tea Cups' or 'Terms & T-Cups'.
The tea theme feels British and may not suit a US insurance and real-estate audience.

round1.name: Under Gable

tagline: Very small heroes. Very short stories.

round1.name: Errandlings
round1.why: 'The small ones sent on big errands' names the whole cast in one easy word, and the logo creature could be called the first Errandling. YouTube's search found no channels with this name.

round1.name: Tall Errands

concerns: Knocked out because the web check couldn't run, so it can't be called safe.

round1.name: Thimble Summit
round1.why: For a creature this size, the top of a thimble is a mountain peak, and planting a flag there is a victory. That matches the logo's flag and the warm, funny sense of scale in every episode.
concerns: Knocked out because the web check couldn't run.
It sounds like a place or an event (a 'summit' can be a conference), and it ties the channel to climbing and peaks. That gives less room to grow than names about the characters.

round1.name: Pluck and Pennant

Hard to type after hearing it once: 'and', '&' or 'n'? 'Pennant' or 'Pennent'? The handle buries the 'and'.
Two old-fashioned words most children won't know. In the US, 'pennant' first brings baseball to mind.
'Pluck' rhymes with a swear word, which can invite playground jokes. That's a small risk, but it is a family brand.

round1.name: Doorstep Odyssey

People often misspell 'Odyssey' ('Odessy', 'Odyssy'), which hurts search and handle typing.

round1.name: Gumption Lane
